title: The Central Limit Theorem
summary: What the CLT says about the sampling distribution of the mean, the n ≥ 30 guideline, why it matters in practice, and the additional reading on an Excel simulation of the theorem.

chunks.heading: What the Central Limit Theorem says
chunks.explanation_md:
The **Central Limit Theorem** states that, for **any population with a finite mean and variance**, the **sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases**, **regardless of the shape of the population distribution**.

This means:

- For **large sample sizes (usually n ≥ 30)**, the **means of repeated samples** will be **approximately normally distributed**.
- The **mean of these sample means equals the population mean**.
- The **variability (standard deviation) decreases** as the sample size increases, because the sample means **cluster more tightly** around the true population mean.

In plain words: take many samples, work out each sample's mean, and those means form a bell curve centred on the true mean, even if the original data was not bell-shaped.

chunks.heading: Why the CLT matters in practice
chunks.explanation_md:
Practical relevance from the slide:

- The **CLT allows the use of normal probability theory even when the original data is not normal**.
- It **enables confidence intervals and hypothesis testing** about population parameters **based on sample data**, even for non-normal populations.
- It is used in **election polling, quality control, finance**, and **estimating average outcomes in populations**.

So everything you learned about the normal curve and z becomes usable for sample means, almost whatever the data looks like.

questions.stem: List the three things the Central Limit Theorem tells us about the means of repeated samples.
questions.model_answer_md:
The CLT gives three practical results about sample means.

- **Shape:** for large samples (usually **n ≥ 30**), the means of repeated samples are **approximately normally distributed**.
- **Centre:** the **mean of the sample means equals the population mean**.
- **Spread:** the **variability (standard deviation) decreases** as the sample size increases, so sample means cluster more tightly around the true population mean.

So bigger samples give sample means that are normal, centred on the truth and less spread out.

questions.stem: Explain the Central Limit Theorem and its practical relevance for managers.
questions.model_answer_md:
Managers rarely see a whole population; they see samples. The **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)** explains how sample means behave, which makes inference from samples possible.

**Statement:** for **any population with a finite mean and variance**, the **sampling distribution of the mean** approaches a **normal distribution** as the **sample size increases**, **regardless of the shape** of the population distribution.

**What this means:**
- **Normal shape:** for large samples (usually **n ≥ 30**), the means of repeated samples are approximately normally distributed.
- **Same centre:** the **mean of the sample means equals the population mean**, so sample means are centred on the truth.
- **Less spread:** the **variability (standard deviation)** of the sample means **decreases** as the sample size increases; they cluster more tightly around the true population mean.

**Practical relevance:**
- It allows the use of **normal probability theory** even when the **original data is not normal**.
- It enables **confidence intervals** and **hypothesis testing** about population parameters from sample data, even for non-normal populations.
- It is used in **election polling, quality control, finance** and **estimating average outcomes** in populations.

**Further reading:** the deck points to an article that uses interactive **Microsoft Excel** simulations to show the CLT's appropriateness for comparing the difference between the means of any two populations.

In short, the CLT is the bridge between a single sample and the whole population: it lets a manager use the normal curve to make reliable statements about averages.

questions.stem: A manager's data come from a population that is clearly not normal. Explain, using the Central Limit Theorem, why the manager can still use the normal distribution and the z table when working with the averages of large samples.
questions.model_answer_md:
The normal distribution and the z table normally need a normal variable. The **Central Limit Theorem** supplies one, even when the raw data are not normal.

**1. The variable changes.** The manager works with the **sample mean**, not single observations. The CLT says that for any population with a **finite mean and variance**, the **sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal distribution** as the sample size grows, **regardless of the population's shape**.

**2. Large samples.** For large samples, **usually n ≥ 30**, the means of repeated samples are approximately normal, so the normal curve's properties apply: it is symmetric, defined by its mean and standard deviation, with total area 1.

**3. Centre and spread.** The **mean of the sample means equals the population mean**, and their **standard deviation decreases** as the sample size increases. So the sample means are centred on the true mean and cluster more tightly around it with bigger samples.

**4. Using z.** Because the sample mean is approximately normal, it can be standardised with **z = (x - μ)/σ** and the standard normal table gives probabilities as areas under the curve.

**5. Why it matters.** This is exactly the practical relevance the deck stresses: the CLT allows **normal probability theory even when the original data is not normal**, and it underpins **confidence intervals and hypothesis tests** in polling, quality control and finance.

So the manager does not need normal data, only a large enough sample, for the normal tools to work on averages.
